clarifying the operation of the tenancy transfer mechanism. The bill already includes a new mechanism to facilitate the transfer of the joint tenancy into the sole name of the victim, where a victim wants to remain in the home as a sole tenant. The bill also includes powers to enable the courts to make an order to provide the victim with suitable alternative accommodation, where it is not appropriate for the victim to remain in a home and the landlord has this accommodation available. The amendments being made to the bill will ensure that where the court makes an order either on the basis that the victim remains in the home as sole tenant or on the basis that they are to be provided with suitable alternative accommodation, then the perpetrator’s interest in the joint tenancy will be brought to an end

Right to Manage reforms

The Right to Manage (RTM) gives local authority tenants a statutory route to take on responsibility for managing housing services through a Tenant Management Organisation (TMO). The government’s response to the Grenfell Tower Inquiry, published in 2025, committed to reviewing oversight arrangements for delegated management organisations, including TMOs.

The review found that the RTM remains an important route for resident control, but that take-up has declined and existing TMOs face growing pressures. Most TMOs are small organisations with limited staffing and volunteer capacity. Stakeholders reported that the set-up process can be complex, access to advice and training is limited, and governance requirements do not always reflect the size, capacity and functions of individual TMOs.

The review also found that roles and responsibilities between TMOs and landlords are not always clear. Management agreements can be outdated and may not reflect current consumer regulation or building safety requirements. Information sharing and performance monitoring are inconsistent, while allowance calculations can be difficult to understand and may not fully reflect rising compliance costs.

The government is therefore bringing forwards amendments to modernise the framework, make it easier for social housing residents to take control of their housing services, and strengthen oversight and accountability. This includes:

broadening regulation-making powers, which will enable clearer and more consistent requirements to be set on matters relating to the ongoing operation of TMOs as well as their setup; these requirements will relate to governance, information sharing, financial management and regulatory compliance

establishing mandatory core requirements on information sharing, ballot arrangements, and conducting reviews, which will be added to existing management agreements. These requirements will bring greater clarity to the respective responsibilities of TMO and local authorities, and consistency with current regulatory requirements, including for building safety and social housing consumer regulations

enabling a tiered governance model to be introduced through regulations. This will ensure that governance, assurance and oversight requirements are proportionate to the scale, complexity and risk of the functions a TMO manages

creating a court-backed intervention route for serious failures. Courts will be able to remove officers, transfer functions, or terminate agreements where necessary and proportionate. This will act as a safeguard of last resort in exceptional cases involving serious governance failures, misconduct or risks to residents’ safety

Tackling homelessness

Duty of private registered provider to offer accommodation after local authority request (Duty to Offer)

In the National Plan to End Homelessness (December 2025), the government committed to considering levers to require social housing landlords to rehouse statutory homeless households referred by the council, where joint working is not operating effectively, including legislating if necessary.

To deliver on this commitment, the government is bringing forward an amendment that will introduce a new statutory power. This power will enable a local housing authority (LHA) to refer a homeless household (owed the main housing duty) to a private registered provider of social housing (PRP), requiring the PRP to offer suitable accommodation to that household, unless they have good reason not to. This measure is designed to strengthen cooperation between LHAs and PRPs and ensure social housing is used effectively to prevent homelessness.

The Secretary of State will set out through regulations what constitutes a reasonable period for making an offer and the circumstances in which a PRP may be regarded as having a good reason not to offer accommodation. We will work with stakeholders to develop these regulations.

Duties of specified bodies to collaborate and act on homelessness

The National Plan to End Homelessness includes a commitment to legislate for a ‘Duty to Collaborate’, to compel public services to work together to prevent homelessness and support those who are at crisis point. The government is delivering on this commitment by introducing several new duties for specified bodies in relation to homelessness.
